extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, campus administrators, and institutional legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory preamble to final Title IX regulations describing required elements, limitations, and implementation expectations for institutional grievance processes (advisors, evidence, confidentiality, standards of proof, timing, definitions of actual knowledge, supportive measures, written determinations, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor cross-examination requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that postsecondary institutions provide an advisor to the parties for the purpose of cross-examination at the live hearing or allow a party to have an advisor who conducts cross-examination at the live hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may prevent an advisor from being disruptive and may implement rules about appropriate conduct; an advisor's role is not limited to an adversarial role and advisors may continue to provide support. Institutions are welcome to provide training to advisors on cross-examination. The Department believes this requirement will lead to a fair, impartial process that will help assess allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct rules for advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may implement rules about appropriate conduct at interviews, meetings, hearings, etc., to require all participants to behave in an orderly manner and to prevent disruptive advisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may limit disruptive behavior while still allowing advisors to support parties; training for advisors is permissible and encouraged to ensure cross-examination is conducted appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of evidence selection and parity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may adopt either a preponderance of the evidence standard or a clear and convincing evidence standard; the Department does not emphasize one standard over another. The only requirement is that recipients use the same standard of evidence for complaints against students as it does for complaints against employees, including faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient cannot require a higher standard of evidence for a student's complaint against an employee than for a student's complaint against another student. The Department declined to require parity of standard across non-sexual-harassment conduct and sexual-harassment conduct; see §106.45(b)(7) and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on litigation-style procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance process under these final regulations does not contain a comprehensive set of rules of evidence, and neither party may issue a subpoena to gather information from each other or the recipient for purposes of the grievance process under §106.45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These regulations are not imposing the same level of process as a Federal district court; absence of court-style evidentiary rules and subpoenas is deliberate to avoid equating campus processes with federal litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of written determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The parties must be informed in writing of 'the result as to each allegation, including a determination regarding responsibility, any sanctions the recipient imposes on the respondent, and whether remedies will be provided by the recipient to the complainant designed to restore or preserve access to the recipient's education program or activity.' Final regulations also require findings of fact supporting the determination under §106.45(b)(7)(ii)(C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parties must receive written notification of results simultaneously. Including findings of fact helps verify that decision-makers exercised independent judgment and did not act with bias; these written determinations serve to ensure that both parties know the factual basis for outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of supportive measures and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The recipient must maintain as confidential any supportive measures provided to the complainant or respondent, 'to the extent that maintaining such confidentiality would not impair the ability of the recipient to provide the supportive measures.' Records of supportive measures under §106.45(b)(10)(C)(ii) are not publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must keep specific supportive measures and the details of remedies confidential (consistent with FERPA); parties will be informed whether remedies will be provided but not the exact remedies. The Title IX rules align with FERPA in protecting education records and the details of accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of reporter identity (retaliation provision)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.71(a) requires a recipient to keep confidential the identity of any individual who has made a report or complaint of sex discrimination (including complainants, respondents, witnesses), except as may be permitted by FERPA or regulations or as required by law or to the extent necessary to carry out the purposes of 34 CFR part 106.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This confidentiality requirement helps address retaliation concerns; exceptions exist where disclosure is required by law or necessary to investigate or adjudicate the complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures: non-punitive, non-disciplinary, and non-unreasonably burdensome
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures must be non-punitive, non-disciplinary, and must not unreasonably burden the other party under §106.30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must offer supportive measures irrespective of whether the complainant files a formal complaint (§106.44(a)). Supportive measures may include housing or class changes and even one-way no-contact orders; however, they cannot be disciplinary sanctions imposed before grievance procedures determine responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer supportive measures regardless of formal complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must offer supportive measures to a complainant irrespective of whether the complainant files a formal complaint (clarified in §106.44(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from Clery Act language that ties accommodations to victim requests; Title IX requires offering supportive measures once the recipient has actual knowledge of sexual harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of non-responsibility and objective evidence evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(1)(iv) presumes respondents are not responsible prior to a determination, but this presumption does not require a recipient to believe a complainant is lying nor does it allow prejudging of facts; credibility determinations cannot be based on a party's status as complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is intended to ensure due process and does not advantage the respondent; recipients must evaluate all relevant evidence objectively and reach determinations without predetermination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt response and reasonably prompt timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient has actual knowledge of sexual harassment in its education program or activity against a person in the U.S., the recipient must respond 'promptly' (§106.44(a)), and §106.45(b)(1)(v) requires recipients to designate reasonably prompt time frames for conclusion of the grievance process including appeals and any informal resolution processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions are intended to ensure investigations are timely and consistent with the Clery Act's requirement that investigations be 'prompt, fair, and impartial,' even though Clery does not specify particular timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'actual knowledge' and authority to institute corrective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department defines 'actual knowledge' in §106.30 as notice to a recipient's Title IX Coordinator, to any official of the recipient who has authority to institute corrective measures on behalf of the recipient, or to any employee of an elementary and secondary school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postsecondary institutions may designate which employees have authority to institute corrective measures so that notice to those employees conveys actual knowledge; mere ability or obligation to report sexual harassment (e.g., being trained to report) does not by itself qualify an individual as having authority to institute corrective measures. Institutions retain discretion to designate confidential resources versus reporting officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to address non-Title IX misconduct via recipient's code of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal of a formal complaint because the conduct does not fall under Title IX jurisdictional requirements does not preclude a recipient from addressing the conduct through the recipient's own code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may use the same grievance process required under §106.45 to address other misconduct; nothing prevents institutions from handling non-Title IX conduct through existing disciplinary mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal access to evidence and disclosure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must have access to evidence; the final regulations require disclosure of evidence to parties and the Department rejects withholding evidence from one party. The proposed rule at §106.45(b)(5)(vi) was interpreted to require that all evidence be disclosed regardless of whether the investigator or decision-maker intends to rely on the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must provide both parties equally accessible versions of records (concerns were raised about searchable vs. non-searchable formats). This diverges from Clery Act practice that permits withholding irrelevant or prejudicial evidence from both parties; Title IX requires broad disclosure for fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may adopt their own definition of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department intentionally does not require recipients to adopt a particular definition of consent with respect to sexual assault; §106.30 clarifies the Assistant Secretary will not require a particular definition of consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing local definitions helps avoid conflicts with State or local laws that may require a recipient to adopt a particular definition of consent; recipients retain discretion to adopt a definition they deem appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator responsibility for implementation of remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(7)(iv) is revised to state that the Title IX Coordinator is responsible for effective implementation of remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a written determination states remedies will be provided to a complainant, the complainant can then communicate separately with the Title IX Coordinator to discuss the nature of such remedies; this centralizes implementation responsibility.
